title: Static Factory Method Pattern
oneLiner: A named static method that builds instances — able to return cached objects or subtypes, something a constructor can never do.

hero.name: The Herald
hero.catchphrase: A name that says what it does, not just 'new'.
hero.power: Constructs objects through a descriptively-named static method that can cache, validate, or return the right subtype — things a bare constructor can't do.
hero.weakness: Static factory methods aren't discoverable through 'implements' the way constructors are conventionally found, and you can't subclass to override construction the way real Factory Method allows.
hero.origin: The Herald appeared after `new Color(255, 0, 0, 255)` left every reader guessing which number was red, green, blue, or alpha — versus `Color.fromHex("#FF0000")`, which explains itself.

story.problem: `new Color(255, 0, 0, 255)` gives no hint which number means what. Every call site needs a comment or a trip to the class definition just to know the argument order.
story.solution: The Herald replaces raw constructor calls with descriptively-named static methods: `Color.fromHex("#FF0000")`, `Color.fromRgb(255, 0, 0)`, `Color.transparent()`. Each name explains exactly what it builds.
story.result: Call sites are self-documenting. `Color.transparent()` can even return the same cached instance every time, instead of allocating a new one for a value that never changes.

before: Constructor calls give no hint what each argument means
Every construction always allocates a brand-new object
Can't return a subtype or cached instance from a constructor
after: Named static methods make intent explicit at the call site
Common values (like transparent) can return a cached instance
A static method can freely return a subtype when appropriate

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A code reviewer squints at new Color(255, 0, 0, 255), unsure which number is which channel.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Is the fourth argument alpha or is it hue? I have to open the Color class every single time to remember.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Herald appears holding a set of clearly labeled banners: fromHex, fromRgb, transparent.
panels.speaker: The Herald
panels.dialogue: Stop naming construction 'new'. Give it a name that says exactly what it builds — fromHex, fromRgb, transparent.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Color.fromHex('#FF0000') and Color.transparent() are static methods, one of which returns a cached shared instance.
panels.speaker: The Herald
panels.dialogue: The name IS the documentation. And transparent() doesn't even need to allocate — it can hand back the same cached instance, every time.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Every call site now reads clearly, with zero need to check the class definition.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Color.fromHex('#FF0000') tells me exactly what it does. No more guessing games at the call site.

useWhen: Multiple meaningful ways exist to construct an object, and each deserves its own descriptive name.
You want to return a cached or shared instance instead of always allocating a fresh one.
You might need to return a subtype of the declared return type, which a constructor can never do.
avoidWhen: There's only one obvious way to construct the object — a plain constructor is simpler and equally clear.
You need the class to be subclassable with construction overridden per-subclass — that's real Factory Method's job, not this idiom's.
Hiding the constructor entirely would surprise developers used to conventional `new ClassName()` discovery.
commonMistakes: Confusing this idiom with GoF's actual Factory Method — Static Factory Method doesn't involve subclassing or an abstract creation method at all.
Forgetting to make the constructor private when the static method is meant to be the only entry point, letting callers bypass caching/validation.
Giving static factory methods vague names (`create()`) instead of descriptive ones (`fromHex()`, `transparent()`) — the whole benefit is a clear name.
Not caching genuinely reusable immutable values (like a shared 'empty' or 'zero' instance), missing an easy allocation win.
explanation.realWorldExample: Java's `Integer.valueOf()` (caches small integers instead of always allocating), `Optional.of()`/`Optional.empty()`, and JavaScript's `Array.from()`/`Object.fromEntries()` are all Static Factory Methods.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this exactly the same as GoF's Factory Method?

conversation.speaker: The Herald
conversation.message: Different tool entirely, despite the similar name. Factory Method uses SUBCLASSES overriding an abstract creation method. I'm just a well-named static method — no subclassing, no abstract method, often on the very class being constructed.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When would I want a subtype returned instead?

conversation.speaker: The Herald
conversation.message: Say `List.of()` — it might return an optimized internal 'immutable list' subtype behind the scenes. Callers only see the interface, `List`. A constructor could never do that; a static method can.

codeBattle.scenario: Your `Optional<T>` value type needs an `empty()` case that's used constantly throughout the codebase, and you want to avoid allocating a fresh 'empty' object every single time it's needed.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Herald's Optional.empty() can return one cached shared instance every time, instead of a constructor that would always allocate fresh.

quiz.question: What can a Static Factory Method do that a plain constructor cannot?
options: Return a cached instance or a subtype, and have a descriptive name
quiz.answer: Return a cached instance or a subtype, and have a descriptive name
quiz.explanation: Constructors always allocate a new instance of exactly the declared class; static factory methods have neither restriction.

quiz.question: How does Static Factory Method differ from GoF's Factory Method pattern?
options: It's a single named static method, with no subclassing or abstract creation method involved
They are the exact same pattern
Static Factory Method requires an interface; Factory Method does not
Factory Method can only be used with primitive types
quiz.answer: It's a single named static method, with no subclassing or abstract creation method involved
quiz.explanation: Despite the similar name, Static Factory Method is a simpler idiom — no abstract method, no subclass hierarchy required.

quiz.question: What's a real benefit of naming a factory method `fromHex()` instead of just using `new Color(...)`?
options: The name documents exactly what the arguments mean and what gets constructed
It makes the code run faster in every case
It removes the need for any constructor at all
quiz.answer: The name documents exactly what the arguments mean and what gets constructed
quiz.explanation: Self-documenting names are the core readability win of this idiom over positional constructor arguments.

quiz.question: What's a common mistake with Static Factory Method?
options: Forgetting to make the constructor private, letting callers bypass caching or validation logic entirely
Giving the method a descriptive name
Returning a cached instance for an immutable value
Using it alongside a private constructor
quiz.answer: Forgetting to make the constructor private, letting callers bypass caching or validation logic entirely
quiz.explanation: If the raw constructor stays public, callers can skip the factory method's benefits (caching, validation) entirely.
